questions.q: How does this lesson's health check differ from Lesson 7's restore test?
options: It only applies to SQL Server on a VM, not Azure SQL Database
It must be run before every single transaction against the database
It replaces the need for ever performing a real restore test
It's a quick, repeatable query to check current status, not a full proof that the backup/restore mechanism works
questions.explain: Lesson 7 proved the restore mechanism works end to end; this lesson is a smaller, faster, repeatable snapshot check of current health, run any time without waiting for an incident.

questions.q: What does WHERE s.is_user_process = 1 accomplish in the sys.dm_exec_sessions query?
options: It filters out SQL Server's own internal system sessions, leaving only real client connections
It shows only sessions that have been idle for over an hour
It limits results to sessions created by the database administrator account only
It restricts the query to only the Patients table
questions.explain: is_user_process = 1 drops internal system sessions so the query shows only real activity from applications and users actually connected to the database.

questions.q: What two practical questions does checking sys.dm_exec_sessions answer at a glance?
options: Is anything actually connected, and does anything look abnormal (like one session using far more CPU than the rest)
Which Azure region the database is deployed in, and its current price tier
Whether Transparent Data Encryption is enabled, and who the database admin is
How much disk space remains, and when the last full backup ran
questions.explain: A quick session check reveals whether expected connections exist and whether any session's resource usage looks unusual — a fast sanity check, not deep diagnostics.

questions.q: How does this lesson's health check confirm the backup chain is current?
options: By querying msdb.dbo.backupset for the last successful job
By checking the Azure subscription's billing history for backup storage charges
By running a manual BACKUP DATABASE statement and checking for errors
By reusing the earliestRestoreDate signal from Lessons 4-6 and checking it looks recent and moving, not stale
questions.explain: The same earliestRestoreDate property used to confirm backups exist in earlier lessons is reused here as a quick, repeatable signal that the chain is still healthy.

questions.q: Why does the lesson deliberately stop at a simple two-part check instead of building a full monitoring dashboard?
options: A simple query is technically impossible to extend into a dashboard
A full alerting/monitoring pipeline is valuable but a different project from what Priya actually asked for in Lesson 1
Dashboards are prohibited by healthcare data compliance rules
Azure SQL Database doesn't support any form of monitoring dashboard
questions.explain: The capstone stays scoped to what was actually asked — a real, tested, documented backup plan — rather than expanding into a separate monitoring/alerting project.
